item.description:
- Artificial intelligence is democratising interference operations
# Artificial intelligence is democratising interference operations Anthropic’s latest threat intelligence report highlights how AI is changing the face of interference and influence operations, levelling the playing field for new actors, and generating novel tactics that outpace counter-interference mechanisms.
In September 2026, Anthropic [released](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/e50be2e51e7695dc4b1366a37a245a597377d3b5/Anthropic-Detecting-and-countering-091026.pdf) an report on attempts to misuse its artificial-intelligence (AI) tools, predominantly the Claude large language model (LLM) and chatbot. This trend has separately been highlighted by [Google](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/adversarial-misuse-generative-ai.pdf) and [OpenAI](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/df438d70-e3fe-4a6c-a403-ff632def8f79/disrupting-malicious-uses-of-ai.pdf), who identified state-backed actors using their AI tools to plan, generate content and amplify covert influence operations in 2025 and early 2026 respectively. Agentic AI is creating entirely new ways of executing influence campaigns and levelling the playing field for non-traditional actors.
### Influence operations – an introduction Anthropic reports that FIMI actors – prominently those originating in Russia and Iran – [used](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/e50be2e51e7695dc4b1366a37a245a597377d3b5/Anthropic-Detecting-and-countering-091026.pdf) its chatbot and LLMs to produce and propagate FIMI through traditional and online media. Separate reporting supports the claims of AI use by Russian state-linked actors in both [Moldova](https://airisk.mit.edu/ai-incidents/1202-russian-disinformation-campaign-reportedly-used-ai) and the [CAR](https://alleyesonwagner.org/2026/07/07/the-svr-arms-politology-with-chatgpt-and-claude-in-the-central-african-republic/).
### New tactics: agentic, autonomous information operations It combines established and emerging techniques with apparently minimal direction, creating a ‘digital twin’ that can act autonomously with broad intent, taking advantage of the [persuasive](https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/130605/) nature of AI chatbots.

Greggor Ilagan, convened a joint informational briefing on Wednesday at the Hawai‘i State Capitol to examine the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI), its role in government operations, and emerging opportunities for workforce development. The joint informational briefing provided a forum for legislators to explore the responsible integration of AI into government operations, identify opportunities for innovation, and examine the safeguards necessary to protect the public. “AI is continuing to advance with new technological developments, and it is critical that we understand AI so that we can develop good policy on privacy, protecting data information, and using AI to promote efficiency,” said Elefante. “Artificial intelligence is already reshaping how we live and work, and it is our responsibility to explore its potential thoughtfully,” said Ilagan. His presentation also explored opportunities to leverage AI as a tool to improve government efficiency. Trung Lam, Executive Director and CEO of the Hawai‘i Technology Development Corporation (HTDC), discussed opportunities to integrate AI into workforce development and prepare Hawai‘i’s workforce for an increasingly technology-driven economy.

item.title: Delphi Study Reveals How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Foundational Human Competencies
item.description:
# Delphi Study Reveals How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Foundational Human Competencies Rather than replacing human labor wholesale, artificial intelligence systems act as collaborative or assistive mechanisms that shift human roles from operational execution toward process orchestration, ethical governance, output evaluation, and strategic problem-solving across contemporary organizational, educational, and professional environments.
Central to the empirical evaluation was an explicit distinction between two operational paradigms of artificial intelligence: weak artificial intelligence and hypothetical strong artificial intelligence. Weak artificial intelligence, encompassing contemporary artificial narrow intelligence platforms such as large language models, ChatGPT, and Gemini, describes task-specific automated systems that execute predefined functions under human guidance without general contextual adaptability or autonomous self-directed problem-solving. In contrast, strong artificial intelligence, or artificial general intelligence, designates hypothetical future computational systems possessing human-comparable intelligence, capable of independent cognitive reasoning, autonomous experience-based learning, and cross-domain flexibility without human supervision.
Critical thinking emerged as the most dramatically elevated competency across the entire investigation; under strong artificial intelligence, 59 percent of academic experts and 94 percent of practitioner experts anticipated strong or very strong positive relevance increases, yielding mean ratings of 2.24 and 2.76 respectively. Analytical thinking, autonomous problem-solving, and systematic decision-making similarly exhibited robust upward trajectories, corroborating theoretical models where routine analytical labor is automated while human responsibility centers on delegating computational tasks, framing systemic questions, and evaluating synthetic outputs.
Digital competency registered substantial positive growth, with 41 percent of academics and 76 percent of corporate practitioners projecting a very strong positive relevance shift under strong artificial intelligence, reflecting the necessity of interfacing directly with complex algorithmic architectures.

item.title: USI receives $8.5 million artificial intelligence grant through Lilly Endowment
item.description:
![USI receives $8.5 million artificial intelligence grant through Lilly Endowment ](https://www.usi.edu/media/lrwhv4fq/cis_-44.jpg?cc=-0.001993986328619963,-0.0029491972450375573,0.003861401259427135,0.0029016767488622606&width=1200&height=800)
# USI receives $8.5 million artificial intelligence grant through Lilly Endowment The three-year grant will support a coordinated University initiative focused on preparing USI graduates to leverage AI responsibly.
The University of Southern Indiana has received an $8.5 million grant from Lilly Endowment Inc. through its Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education (AIHE) initiative. USI will use the grant funding to prepare students, faculty and staff to thrive in a world increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence.
The three-year grant will support a coordinated University initiative focused on preparing USI graduates to leverage AI responsibly and ethically and make positive contributions to their communities.
USI will develop multiple curricular, co-curricular and experiential pathways for students to build general and discipline-specific AI fluency, while also strengthening faculty and staff AI capacity, AI infrastructure, student support and academic operations.
“This investment gives USI an extraordinary opportunity to prepare our students not simply to use AI, but to understand how and when to use it responsibly and effectively within their disciplines and future careers,” said Dr. Shelly Blunt, Provost. “It will also give our faculty and staff the time, resources and support needed to thoughtfully examine what AI means for teaching, learning and student success while keeping critical thinking, human judgment, creativity and ethical decision-making at the center of a USI education.”
The work builds on a December 2025 Phase 1 planning grant from Lilly Endowment Inc. that helped the University assess its most compelling needs regarding AI, consider the most promising ideas to help address them and prepare an implementation grant proposal.
USI is among 35 Indiana colleges and universities receiving implementation grants through Lilly Endowment Inc.’s AIHE initiative. The grants, ranging from $2.5 million to $25 million, total nearly $292 million and are based on student enrollment at each institution. The Endowment has allocated $500 million for the initiative, including planning grants, implementation grants and large-scale collaborative grants.
During the planning phase, USI assessed regional workforce needs, AI topics in the curriculum and AI use in instruction while providing professional development opportunities for faculty and staff.
Employers identified basic AI literacy, AI-assisted communication and ethical and legal use of AI among skills expected of new hires across work roles.
The grant will support eight interconnected projects, including:
- **Develop Faculty and Staff AI Fluency:** USI will strengthen faculty and staff AI capacity through professional development, communities of practice, showcases, self-paced training, discipline-specific learning funds and protected time and compensation for deeper AI-related curriculum and program improvement. - **Leveraging AI to Improve Academic Operational Effectiveness and Efficiency:** USI will leverage AI tools to streamline and improve academic operations, understanding that speeding core processes enables better facilitation of student success.
_Lilly and his sons, Eli and J.K._
